title: Water system upgrades and retrofits, any builder | Aquemi
meta: Upgrade a PW or WFI system from any builder: RO/EDI, sanitization, online TOC, Part 11 controls, dead legs, with the EU GMP Annex 15 requalification scope.
eyebrow: UPGRADES · RETROFITS · ANY BUILDER · EU GMP ANNEX 15 · 21 CFR PART 11 · ASME BPE
headline: Upgrade the water system you already have, with the requalification scope known before the first cut
lead: Most upgrade projects that overrun do so in validation, not in fabrication: a controls swap that turns into a full software revalidation, a new branch that moves the coldest point of the loop, a route change nobody told the regulator about. We start with an assessment of your Purified Water (PW), Water for Injection (WFI) or pure steam system, whoever built it, and give you each option with its downtime and the installation, operational and performance qualification (IQ, OQ, PQ) it triggers under EU GMP Annex 15, section 11, before you raise the change request.
primary_cta_intent: Assessment of an existing system, any make

secondary_cta.label: Water out of specification or system down now? Request service

blocks.h: Your system is older than its controls and younger than the rules it is now judged by
body: A PW or WFI system installed fifteen years ago was qualified against the expectations of its day. Since then the revised EU GMP Annex 1 (2022, in force from August 2023 and adopted by Health Canada as GUI-0119) has asked for continuous total organic carbon (TOC) and conductivity monitoring on WFI systems, a sanitization schedule set from monitoring results and a contamination control strategy that covers water. Data integrity expectations under 21 CFR Part 11 and EU GMP Annex 11 have reached the controls cabinet. And the programmable logic controller (PLC) that runs the system may now be a part its maker no longer sells.

None of that forces a new system. It forces decisions, and each decision has two costs: the work itself and the requalification that follows it. Annex 15, section 11 asks that every planned change is assessed for its effect on the qualified state before it is made, and WHO TRS 1033 Annex 3 allows the PQ phases and their length for a change to an existing system to be set by documented risk assessment rather than repeated in full. Used well, that saves months. Used badly, it produces either a short PQ an inspector questions or a full year of sampling nobody needed.

So we price the requalification with the work. Every option in an assessment report states what changes physically, which documents and tests it touches, how long the water is unavailable, and how you keep supplying production while it is done.

blocks.h: Common upgrades, and the requalification scope to plan for each

rows.t: Chemical deionization (DI) to reverse osmosis (RO) and electrodeionization (EDI)

rows: Remove acid and caustic regeneration or exchange-tank deliveries, get steadier conductivity, and take resin beds that stand at ambient temperature out of the generation step
New generation skid, pretreatment matched to RO (chlorine removal, softening, antiscalant), new drain and reject routing; the loop usually stays

IQ and OQ of the new generation skid, leveraging factory acceptance tests (FAT) where your quality unit accepts them. Intensive sampling after each step, at the loop return and at points of use for a risk-assessed period, then a reduced plan; alert levels reviewed on the new data
Annex 15, section 11; WHO TRS 1033 Annex 3, 11.3

rows.t: Hot water sanitization on an ambient loop

rows: Replace chemical sanitization, or meet Annex 1, 6.12 with a schedule your data support

Loop heater on a sanitary double tube sheet heat exchanger, temperature probes at the coldest points, heated vent filter, allowance for expansion; every component checked for its rating at the sanitization temperature

IQ of the new equipment and of material and pressure ratings. OQ of the full cycle with temperature recorded at the coldest probe for the hold time, then sampling long enough to show control at the new frequency
USP <1231> (65–80 °C commonly used); Annex 1, 6.12

rows.t: Ozone and destruct UV on an ambient loop

rows: Sanitize PW or membrane WFI loops without heat cycles, or loops whose piping is not rated for heat

Ozone generator and injection at the tank, 254 nm ultraviolet (UV) destruct before the loop supply, dissolved ozone sensors in the tank, after the UV and on the return, ozone-compatible seals and diaphragms, a room gas monitor and a safe vent route

IQ, including an elastomer compatibility review. OQ of the tank ozone set point, of ozone absent after the UV and at points of use before release, and of the loop sanitization with the UV off. Intensive microbial sampling through the first sanitization intervals
ISPE Baseline Guide Vol. 4 (0.02–0.2 ppm); Annex 1, 6.12

rows.t: Online TOC and conductivity, or real-time release

rows: Annex 1, 6.15 expects continuous TOC and conductivity on WFI; online release cuts laboratory load
Analyzer and sample line at the risk-based location, data path to the PLC or historian, alarms

IQ of the instrument and data path. OQ including USP <643> system suitability (85–115 %) and audit trail checks. A period of parallel online and laboratory results before your quality unit moves release to the online value

rows.t: PLC, operator panel (HMI) and SCADA replacement

rows: End-of-life hardware, unpatched operating systems, no audit trail, shared logins, paper chart recorders
New controller and panel, rewritten or converted logic, new historian or electronic records, often new instruments on digital communication

Computerized system validation under GAMP 5: specifications, risk assessment, software FAT on a simulator, IQ of hardware and software, OQ of every sequence, alarm and interlock, data integrity tests, and migration or retention of legacy records. Short water sampling after cutover where the process itself is unchanged
21 CFR Part 11; EU GMP Annex 11; GAMP 5

rows.t: Dead leg removal and loop modifications

rows: Branches beyond the ASME BPE target of L/D ≤ 2, abandoned outlets, inspection findings
Branches cut out, new zero-static point-of-use valves, orbital welds, slope corrected, new piping cleaned and passivated

IQ of the modified section (weld map and log, borescope records, slope, L/D, passivation). Updated isometrics and dead leg register. OQ of sanitization if the coldest point moves, and intensive sampling at the affected and neighbouring points
ASME BPE; Annex 1, 6.7; WHO TRS 1033 Annex 3
New products, a new suite, or a generator that no longer refills the tank between peaks
Second RO train or larger skid, larger tank, bigger loop pump or a new sub-loop; pretreatment rechecked at the new flow and the coldest feed temperature

IQ and OQ of new equipment. OQ of loop hydraulics at the new peak draw, with return flow and pressure inside the design range. For a new tank, spray device coverage. Sampling at new points of use and at the points nearest the change
Annex 1, 6.9; Annex 15, section 11

rows.t: Changing the WFI route: distillation to membrane, or back

rows: Steam cost or availability, energy targets, or a move to hot WFI or to a market that calls for distillation
New generation system, usually built alongside the existing one; storage temperature and sanitization reviewed with the route

Full IQ and OQ of the new generator and a three-phase PQ at generation and points of use, with the existing still or skid kept as supply until your quality unit releases the new water. For membrane WFI in Ph. Eur. markets, notice to your GMP supervisory authority before implementation
Ph. Eur. 0169; EMA/INS/GMP/443117/2017; WHO TRS 1033 Annex 3
Rouge remediation
Visible rouge on tank walls, spray devices or hot loop surfaces; inspection findings
Derouging and repassivation of the affected surfaces, with surfaces inspected before and after
Cleaning and passivation records reviewed under change control, return-to-service flushing with conductivity and TOC checks, then closer sampling for a short period
ASME BPE; [passivation standard used, e.g. ASTM A967 or ASTM A380]
Full replacement
A system beyond economic repair, or several of the upgrades above at once
New generation, storage and distribution, built alongside the old system where space allows
As a new system: FAT, commissioning, IQ, OQ and a three-phase PQ to at least 12 months, with cutover planned so the old system supplies production until release

blocks.h: We size requalification by what the change can affect, not by habit
blocks.body: For each option we list the critical aspects the change can reach: water quality at generation, in the loop and at the points of use, the sanitization cycle, and the data your release depends on. Anything outside that reach is left alone, and the reasoning goes into the change impact assessment so your quality unit can sign it and an inspector can follow it. Where the risk assessment is borderline, we say so and propose the longer sampling period.

blocks.h: Systems whose builder has changed hands
body: Many PW and WFI systems in service in North America were built by companies that have since been sold, merged or renamed. Evoqua became part of Xylem in 2023, a year after buying the renal business that Mar Cor and Cantel had operated under STERIS. Grundfos agreed to acquire MECO in 2021 and completed its acquisition of Newterra in 2025. Ecolab bought Ovivo's electronics ultrapure water business in 2025. Systems keep running through changes like these. What tends to change is who answers the phone, which part numbers are current, and who still holds the software.

We work on systems we did not build. [Confirm the equipment types and makes Aquemi services and upgrades.] The first step is the same as for our own: an assessment of the system as it stands and of the records behind it, so that every later replacement is checked like for like against a known original, and every upgrade starts from a drawing that matches the pipework.

body: EDI module makers present continuous electrodeionization as a chemical-free alternative to mixed-bed DI with lower operating and maintenance cost. Whether that holds for your plant depends on your water volume, your exchange-tank or chemical cost, your drain charges and your power cost, so the assessment works the comparison out per cubic metre of water for your system rather than quoting a percentage. blocks.h: Obsolete controllers: replace them before the last spare is used
body: Several controller families common on water systems are discontinued or in phase-out, for example Allen-Bradley PLC-5 and SLC 500 and Siemens S5 and S7-300. Replacing the controller is never like for like: even a converted program is new software under Annex 11 and GAMP 5, and every sequence, alarm and interlock is tested again. We build the new panel and test the program against a simulator at our shop, so site work is the swap, the IQ and the OQ, in a window of [controls swap window, days]. Monitoring and controls describes the validated architecture we replace them with.

Since 1 April 2017, Ph. Eur. 0169 accepts WFI made by reverse osmosis coupled with other suitable techniques, and USP has long allowed any process equivalent or superior to distillation. A move from a still to membrane WFI saves plant steam and cooling water, but it replaces one phase change with several barriers in series and a documented control strategy, as the EMA questions and answers on non-distillation WFI (EMA/INS/GMP/443117/2017) expect. For Ph. Eur. markets it also needs notice to your GMP supervisory authority before implementation.

The move can run the other way. A site that needs hot WFI for a hot loop, or that supplies a market or works to a corporate standard that still calls for distillation, may replace a membrane skid with a still. In both directions we build the new generator alongside the old one where space allows, so the existing system supplies production until your quality unit releases the new water, and the route assessment checks every market you release into. Ask your regulatory team whether your marketing authorizations or site master file describe the WFI route; if they do, the change may need a filing as well as change control.

blocks.h: Questions engineering, validation and quality teams ask

items.q: Our system was built by another supplier. Will you work on it?
items.a: [Confirm scope.] Yes, starting with an assessment. We need whatever records you have. Where drawings, the PLC program or the qualification file are missing, the assessment report lists what to recover and what it costs to recreate it, before any upgrade is designed.

items.q: Will an upgrade restart our PQ from zero?
items.a: Not usually. WHO TRS 1033 Annex 3 allows the PQ phases and their length after a change to an existing system to be set by documented risk assessment. A new generation step or a route change justifies an intensive phase; a new branch justifies sampling at that branch and its neighbours; a controller swap with the process unchanged may justify only short sampling after cutover. Your quality unit decides; we write the rationale it needs.

items.q: Can we keep producing water during the upgrade?
items.a: Usually. Most generation upgrades are built alongside the running system and tied in during a short shutdown. Loop work needs a planned shutdown, followed by sanitization and sampling before release, so we plan it against your production schedule and your storage volume. Where the shutdown is longer than storage can cover, the options say so.

items.q: Is a PLC replacement really a full revalidation?
items.a: Of the control system, yes, because the software is new even when the logic is converted. Of the water system, no: if sequences, set points and equipment are unchanged, the process qualification stands and the water sampling after cutover is short. Testing the software against a simulator before site work keeps the on-site part of that validation short.

items.q: We cannot get the PLC program or passwords from the original supplier.
items.a: Then a modification cannot be validated, and we plan a replacement. We document the running system first, from its inputs and outputs, observed sequences, set points and alarms and your functional requirements, so the new program is specified from evidence rather than memory.

items.q: Does adding ozone or hot water sanitization change our microbial limits?
items.a: No. Limits come from the pharmacopoeia and your specification. What changes is how the system holds them, so the OQ proves the new cycle at the coldest or most remote point, and the sampling period afterwards shows the new frequency works. Alert levels are then reviewed on the new data.

items.q: Do we need to tell a regulator about the change?
items.a: For most upgrades, change control is enough. The exceptions to check are a move to membrane WFI, where Ph. Eur. 0169 asks for notice to your GMP supervisory authority before implementation, and any change to something your marketing authorization or site master file describes. Your regulatory team decides; we supply the technical documents behind it.

items.q: What does an assessment cost, and is it worth it if we already know what we want?
items.a: [Assessment price or 'from' price, CAD, and whether it is credited against the upgrade.] Even a known upgrade needs the as-built state, the data and the requalification scope to be priced properly.
